The GCs with extended HB are more massive than normal GCs, and are dominated by random motion with no correlation between kinematics and metallicity. Our result further suggests heterogeneous origins of GCs, and we anticipate this to be a starting point for more detailed investigations of Milky Way formation, including early mergers, collapse, and later accretion.

# The Origins of Milky Way Globular Clusters: Evidence for Heterogeneous Formation

## Extended Horizontal Branches and Helium-Enhanced Populations

Approximately 25% of the globular clusters in the Milky Way display unusually extended color distributions along their horizontal branches. This distinctive feature is now understood to result from the presence of helium-enhanced second-generation subpopulations within these clusters. The existence of such subpopulations points to a unique formation history, distinguishing these objects from the broader population of globular clusters and offering important clues about their origin.

## Distinct Properties of Extended Horizontal-Branch Clusters

Globular clusters that exhibit extended horizontal branches stand apart from normal clusters in several fundamental respects. They tend to be more massive, and their internal dynamics are dominated by random motion rather than ordered rotation. Notably, these clusters show no correlation between their kinematics and their metallicity. Taken together, these characteristics mark them as a genuinely distinct class of objects, whose properties cannot be explained by the same processes that shaped the majority of globular clusters.

## Evidence for Dissipational Collapse Among Normal Inner Halo Clusters

When the extended horizontal-branch clusters are set aside, a clearer picture emerges for the remaining population. Most normal globular clusters located in the inner halo display distinct signatures of dissipational collapse. This process—in which gas radiates away energy and settles into a more ordered configuration—apparently played a central role in the formation of the Galactic disk. The kinematic and chemical properties of these inner halo clusters are therefore consistent with an in-situ origin tied to the early collapse and structuring of the Milky Way.

## Accretion Origins for Outer Halo Clusters

In contrast, the normal globular clusters found in the outer halo share kinematic properties with the extended horizontal-branch clusters. This similarity is consistent with an accretion origin, in which these clusters were not formed within the Milky Way itself but were instead captured from smaller satellite systems that merged with the Galaxy over time. Their dynamical behavior thus reflects a history of external acquisition rather than internal formation.

## Implications for Understanding Milky Way Formation

Collectively, these findings indicate that globular clusters do not share a single, uniform origin. Instead, they arise from a variety of formation pathways, reflecting the complex assembly history of the Galaxy. This heterogeneity provides a valuable starting point for investigating how the Milky Way came to be, encompassing early mergers, dissipational collapse, and the later accretion of external systems. By disentangling these distinct populations, researchers can build a more complete and nuanced understanding of the processes that shaped our Galaxy over cosmic time.

# Extended Horizontal-Branch Globular Clusters: Distinct Kinematics and Mass as Tracers of Milky Way Formation

## Introduction

Globular clusters are among the oldest stellar systems in the Milky Way, and as such they preserve valuable information about the conditions under which our Galaxy first assembled. Traditionally regarded as simple stellar populations, globular clusters have in recent years been revealed to host complex internal chemistry, including multiple stellar generations characterized by distinct light-element abundances. One striking manifestation of this internal complexity is found in the morphology of the horizontal branch, the region of the color-magnitude diagram populated by evolved, core helium-burning stars.

Approximately one-quarter of the globular clusters in the Milky Way display horizontal branches that are unusually extended in color. This peculiar morphology is widely attributed to the presence of helium-enhanced second-generation subpopulations. When a fraction of a cluster's stars form from material enriched in helium by earlier generations, their evolutionary tracks shift, producing hotter, bluer horizontal-branch stars that stretch the overall color distribution. These extended horizontal-branch (EHB) clusters therefore represent a distinctive class whose formation histories may differ fundamentally from those of ordinary clusters.

## Aims of the Study

The central question addressed by this investigation is whether these peculiar EHB clusters are simply a variant of the normal globular cluster population or whether they constitute a genuinely distinct group with different physical origins. To answer this, the study compares the two populations across two key dimensions: their kinematics, which encode the dynamical history and orbital properties inherited from the epoch of formation, and their masses, which reflect the conditions required to retain enriched gas and form multiple generations of stars.

## Results

The analysis uncovers systematic differences between the two classes of clusters. The extended horizontal-branch clusters are found to be systematically more massive than their normal counterparts. This elevated mass is physically significant, since a deeper gravitational potential well would allow a cluster to retain the ejecta of first-generation stars and subsequently form a helium-enriched second generation. In this sense, the greater mass of EHB clusters is consistent with their proposed multiple-population nature.

Beyond mass, the kinematics of the two populations diverge in an illuminating way. The EHB clusters are dominated by random motion, exhibiting a pressure-supported, dynamically hot distribution with little evidence of organized rotation. Such kinematic behavior is characteristic of systems that either formed in a chaotic, dissipationless manner or were later accreted into the Galactic halo from external progenitors.

In contrast, the normal clusters located in the inner halo display clear signatures of dissipational collapse. Their orbital properties point toward a coherent, rotationally supported configuration consistent with the gradual settling of gas into a flattened, disk-like structure. This pattern is exactly what one would expect if these clusters formed during the rapid, dissipative collapse of the early proto-Galaxy, in which gas radiated away energy, spun up, and organized itself into the beginnings of the Galactic disk.

## Discussion and Implications

Taken together, these findings indicate that the Milky Way's globular cluster system is heterogeneous in origin. The two populations—extended horizontal-branch clusters on the one hand, and normal inner-halo clusters on the other—appear to trace distinct formation channels. The dissipationless, pressure-supported EHB clusters may represent systems built up through early mergers or acquired through the later accretion of satellite galaxies, while the normal, rotationally supported clusters reflect the in-situ dissipational collapse that shaped the inner Galaxy.

This distinction provides a valuable framework for reconstructing the assembly history of the Milky Way. By using globular clusters as fossil tracers, one can begin to disentangle the interplay of the major processes thought to have governed Galactic formation: the early mergers of subgalactic fragments, the dissipative collapse that produced the disk, and the ongoing accretion of external systems that continues to build up the halo. The recognition that EHB and normal clusters carry different kinematic and structural imprints thus lays the groundwork for a more complete and physically motivated picture of how our Galaxy came to be.

# The Milky Way

The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our solar system, Earth, and everything we can see in the night sky with the naked eye. This vast collection of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter has fascinated humans for thousands of years, appearing as a hazy band of light stretching across the heavens.

## What Is the Milky Way?

The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy, meaning it has a central bar-shaped structure surrounded by winding arms of stars. Scientists estimate that our galaxy contains between 100 and 400 billion stars, along with countless planets, nebulae, and other celestial objects. Despite its enormous size, spanning approximately 100,000 light-years in diameter, it is just one of trillions of galaxies in the observable universe.

## Our Place in the Galaxy

Our solar system is located in one of the spiral arms, known as the Orion Arm, about 27,000 light-years from the galactic center. At the heart of the Milky Way lies a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A*, which has a mass equivalent to about four million times that of our Sun. Everything in the galaxy, including our Sun, orbits around this central point, with our solar system taking roughly 230 million years to complete a single orbit.

## The Name and Its Origins

The name "Milky Way" comes from its milky appearance in the sky. Ancient Greeks called it "galaxias kyklos," meaning "milky circle," which is where the word "galaxy" originates. Many cultures throughout history have developed their own myths and stories to explain this glowing river of light.

## Observing the Milky Way

On clear, dark nights away from city lights, the Milky Way appears as a faint, cloudy band arching across the sky. What we are actually seeing is the combined light of billions of distant stars in the galactic plane. Unfortunately, light pollution has made it increasingly difficult for people in urban areas to witness this natural wonder.

## Conclusion

The Milky Way is more than just our cosmic address—it is a reminder of the vastness and beauty of the universe. As technology advances, scientists continue to uncover new secrets about our galaxy, deepening our understanding of where we come from and our place among the stars.

# Abstract

Globular clusters (GCs) exhibiting extended horizontal-branch (EHB) morphologies represent a distinct subpopulation whose formation and evolutionary histories remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the kinematic and structural properties of Milky Way GCs with extended horizontal branches and compare them systematically to the general GC population. Using a sample of Galactic globular clusters drawn from *Gaia* astrometry and complementary spectroscopic catalogs, we characterize their orbital parameters, velocity dispersions, spatial distributions, and dynamical masses. We find that EHB clusters are preferentially more massive than normal GCs, with a median mass exceeding that of the comparison sample by a significant margin, consistent with the hypothesis that a critical mass threshold is required to retain enriched material and sustain multiple stellar generations. Kinematically, EHB clusters display distinct orbital signatures, including a tendency toward more bound, inner-halo orbits and lower orbital eccentricities relative to the broader GC population, suggesting a connection to early *in situ* formation and/or accretion from massive progenitor systems. We further identify correlations between horizontal-branch extension, internal velocity dispersion, and helium enrichment, supporting a scenario in which EHB morphology is linked to the presence of chemically anomalous, helium-enhanced second-generation stars in dynamically evolved, high-mass clusters. Our results reinforce the interpretation that extended horizontal branches serve as a photometric tracer of a cluster's mass, multiple-population content, and assembly history within the Galaxy. We discuss the implications of these findings for models of GC self-enrichment and for reconstructing the hierarchical build-up of the Milky Way halo.

---

## The Dual Origin of the Milky Way Globular Cluster System: Kinematic and Structural Evidence from Extended Horizontal-Branch Clusters

**Abstract**

We present an analysis of the Galactic globular cluster (GC) population aimed at disentangling the *in situ* and accreted components of the Milky Way's cluster system. Using a combination of horizontal-branch (HB) morphology, kinematics, and cluster mass estimates, we identify extended-HB globular clusters as a kinematically and structurally distinct subpopulation. These systems occupy a separate locus in mass–morphology space, exhibiting systematically higher masses than their normal-HB counterparts, and display coherent kinematic signatures that set them apart from the canonical GC population. The extended-HB clusters, distinguished by their mass and kinematics, represent a key tracer of the accretion history and may constitute the surviving cores of these merged systems.

counterfactuals.output:
# Helium-Enhanced Second-Generation Populations and Extended Horizontal Branches: Constraints on Milky Way Assembly

**Abstract**

Multiple stellar populations are now recognized as a defining characteristic of globular clusters (GCs), with second-generation (2G) stars exhibiting enhanced helium abundances (ΔY up to ~0.05–0.13) alongside distinctive light-element anticorrelations (Na-O, Mg-Al). We investigate the connection between helium-enriched 2G subpopulations and the morphology of extended horizontal branches (EHBs) across a sample of Galactic GCs, examining how internal enrichment histories map onto observable photometric and spectroscopic diagnostics. Helium enhancement systematically shifts 2G stars toward hotter, bluer horizontal branch loci, naturally reproducing the blue tails and multimodal distributions observed in massive clusters such as ω Centauri, NGC 2808, and NGC 6388. By coupling He-abundance spreads with mass-loss prescriptions along the red giant branch, we demonstrate that EHB extent serves as a sensitive tracer of the fraction and enrichment level of 2G material retained during cluster formation.

We further explore the implications of these signatures for the hierarchical assembly of the Milky Way. Clusters displaying pronounced He-enhanced populations and complex EHB morphologies preferentially exhibit kinematics and metallicities consistent with an accreted origin, linking them to disrupted dwarf-galaxy progenitors (e.g., Gaia-Enceladus, Sagittarius). We argue that the interplay of **in situ collapse**, **major mergers**, and **satellite accretion** imprints distinguishable chemical and structural fingerprints on the GC population: in situ clusters trace the rapid dissipative collapse of the proto-Galaxy, whereas accreted systems retain the enrichment signatures of their host environments. Our results support a scenario in which helium-enhanced multiple populations and their horizontal-branch manifestations constitute a fossil record of Galactic assembly, offering an independent chronometer and chemodynamical probe complementary to field-star surveys. We discuss prospects for disentangling these formation channels with next-generation astrometric and high-resolution spectroscopic datasets.

*Keywords:* globular clusters — horizontal branch — stellar abundances — Galaxy: formation — Galaxy: halo — multiple stellar populations

# Abstract

The formation and assembly history of the Galactic globular cluster system remains a subject of active debate, with mounting evidence suggesting that these stellar systems arise from multiple distinct evolutionary channels rather than a single monolithic process. In this study, we investigate the heterogeneous origins of globular clusters by examining the interplay between their internal chemical and dynamical properties. We identify a population of massive clusters characterized by extended horizontal branches (HB) whose stellar kinematics are dominated by random motion, exhibiting isotropic velocity dispersions and weak or absent rotational signatures. These systems, which often display complex multiple stellar populations and extended chemical abundance spreads, are consistent with an accreted origin from disrupted dwarf galaxies or the remnant nuclei of more massive progenitor systems, decoupling their present-day dynamics from the ambient Galactic potential. In marked contrast, we find that normal globular clusters exhibit pronounced correlations between metallicity and kinematics, wherein the more metal-rich clusters preferentially trace ordered rotation aligned with the Galactic disk, while metal-poor counterparts populate the extended halo with predominantly pressure-supported orbits. This metallicity–kinematics coupling is naturally explained by in-situ formation coeval with the assembly of the proto-Galactic components. Taken together, our results provide compelling evidence that the globular cluster system comprises at least two dynamically and chemically distinct subpopulations, underscoring the dual role of accretion and in-situ formation in shaping the Galactic halo and offering critical constraints on hierarchical models of galaxy assembly.
